object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier from whom the organization procures goods or services. Identified by a unique vendor number and tracked through onboarding, review, and classification processes.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master... Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
Every vendor has exactly one, and no two vendors share one?... Yes. That one I'm sure about. It's the thing we quote in every conversation with AP.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: The unique system identifier assigned to a vendor upon creation.

source_references.excerpt: Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The official registered name of the vendor organization.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

object_types.name: TaxID
object_types.definition: The tax identification number (e.g., W-9) associated with the vendor. Not a unique identifier; multiple vendors may share the same tax ID.

source_references.excerpt: Could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead?... You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

object_types.name: Address
object_types.definition: A location address associated with a vendor (remit-to, ship-from, or legal).

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The operational state of a vendor record.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended... Collapsed into three, yes. Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: A classification based on procurement spend with the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold... I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: A classification based on the compliance risk assessment of the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high... And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A formal risk assessment of a vendor, completed and signed off by compliance. A vendor may accumulate multiple reviews over time; at most one is the current signed-off review at any moment.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review. Not zero, and the one has to be signed off... A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one. But one of them is the current signed-off one.
The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: ReviewID
object_types.definition: The unique system identifier for a risk review record.

source_references.excerpt: It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: Region
object_types.definition: A geographic area served by vendors, identified by a region code.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM... Four regions, fixed?... Four today. There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened.

object_types.name: RegionCode

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM... Four today.

ambiguities.description: Multiple addresses per vendor: The transcript states vendors have three types of addresses (remit-to, ship-from, legal) that are frequently different. The current model treats Address as a generic value type without distinguishing address types. It is unclear whether the model should (a) create separate fact types for each address type, (b) include an AddressType dimension to the fact type, or (c) keep addresses generic and document the three types informally.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Risk Tier assignment: The transcript indicates risk tier is 'set by the review' but does not explicitly state whether the Review record itself stores the tier value or whether it is a separate attribute. It is unclear if risk tier should be modeled as a property of RiskReview or as a separate assignment from RiskReview to Vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier. Draft vendors don't have one... It's set by the review. A vendor with no review has no risk tier.

ambiguities.description: Current vs. historical reviews: The transcript mentions that a vendor accumulates reviews over time and 'at most one is the current one,' but does not explicitly define how the system marks a review as 'current.' It is unclear whether there is a separate 'is current' flag, a timestamp-based rule, or another mechanism to identify the current signed-off review.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one. But one of them is the current signed-off one... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.

ambiguities.description: Contact information completeness: The transcript states that vendor contact information includes 'Name, email, phone number' in a regional context, but does not clarify whether all three (name, email, phone) are mandatory or optional. The current model treats Contact, Email, and PhoneNumber as separate value types in separate ternary facts, but it is unclear if a vendor-region pair must have all three or if some can be absent.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number... Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID constraint: The transcript indicates that multiple vendors can share the same tax ID due to parent company structures or duplicate onboardings, but does not define a rule about maximum cardinality (many-to-one vs. no constraint). It is unclear whether the absence of uniqueness on TaxID should be explicitly modeled as a constraint or left implicit.

source_references.excerpt: Could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead?... You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

ambiguities.description: Vendor-PurchaseOrder eligibility: The transcript states that a PO can be raised against an active vendor only, but the exact enforcement mechanism and any temporal behavior (what happens if a vendor transitions after PO creation) is not explicitly addressed. The control at PO creation is mentioned, but post-creation state transitions are noted as an unresolved policy issue.

source_references.excerpt: A PO is raised against exactly one vendor, and you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active... Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Tier field overloading: The transcript reveals that both procurement (spend tier) and compliance (risk tier) use the term 'tier' for different classifications, and stakeholders have struggled to eliminate the ambiguity despite efforts. While the model now treats them as separate fields, the business process and user interface may still conflate them. It is unclear whether a UI/documentation change is needed or if the data model separation suffices.

source_references.excerpt: That's not the tier I use... I use low, medium, high... We've asked people to say spend tier and risk tier. Nobody does. It's been a losing battle for two years.

ambiguities.description: Vendor operational scope: The transcript indicates that most vendors operate in only one region, while large vendors operate in multiple regions. There is no explicit constraint on which regions a vendor must or may operate in, nor is there a rule preventing a vendor from operating in zero regions. It is unclear whether the absence of a vendor-region pair should be treated as undefined or whether it means the vendor does not operate in that region.

source_references.excerpt: And can a vendor have no contact in a region?... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Legal Name uniqueness: The transcript uses 'name' and 'legal name' when discussing vendor identification, but states that by default vendors are identified 'by name, usually,' not by legal name as a formal identifier. It is unclear whether legal name is unique, should be unique, or is merely descriptive. A business rule about legal name uniqueness has not been stated.

source_references.excerpt: How do you tell one vendor from another?... By name, usually... Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
